offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: No tool calls are left; the evidence points to fake-provider failing and timing out, which opened payments-api's circuit breaker.

findings.cause: From about 18:53Z fake-provider began failing /v1/payments calls. Some came back as fast HTTP 500s, and others hung until payments-api's 3 s client read timeout. payments-api retries up to 3 times, about 3 s each, so a request could take up to about 9.6 s. That explains the 3.7 s p95. As failures piled up, payments-api's provider circuit breaker (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on) opened at about 18:54:20Z. Since then nearly every POST /payments gets an immediate 503 ('/v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open'), and the payment is left pending. That is the 97% 5xx rate. The breaker is working as designed. The root failure is at the provider (an outside party), not a recent change of ours.

evidence.shows: POST /payments: 201s fall from about 3.4/s to 0, and 503s rise from about 0.1/s to 12.7/s between 18:54:21 and 18:54:51Z. The alert's symptom is real.
All recent payments-api ERROR lines say 'provider unavailable; payment left pending': the circuit breaker is open and the provider call is not sent.
Provider calls with an HTTP answer include 500s at about 0.27-0.40/s from 18:52:57Z. All calls drop to 0 once the breaker opens. ReadTimeouts are not counted under these labels.
Slowest trace (pmt_000252, 9.6 s, 503): Redis and Postgres take under 2 ms. Three POSTs to fake-provider /v1/payments each end in httpx ReadTimeout after about 3.0 s.
POST /payments traces at 18:53:58-18:54:04Z took 3.0, 6.2 and 9.6 s, matching 1-3 timed-out attempts of about 3 s each.
Provider calls that did return took about 5-8 ms at p95. The provider was either fast or hung until our timeout; it was not uniformly slow.
Provider attempts rise to about 3.9/s by 18:54Z, then fall to about 0.08/s by 18:55Z. Only the breaker's trial calls are left.

All containers were created at 18:52:28-29Z from the same image. payments-api has PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=returned. No change shortly before the failure began.

proposed.why: The tool results support the investigator's account: the provider failed and hung, and our circuit breaker turned that into fast 503s. No listed action fits, because no change of ours is implicated.

diagnosis.hypothesis: fake-provider, which stands for the outside payment provider, began failing POST /v1/payments. Some calls got fast HTTP 500s from the first scrape (18:52:57Z). By about 18:53:58Z other calls hung until payments-api's roughly 3 s client read timeout. payments-api retries up to 3 times, so a request could take about 9.6 s, which explains the 3.7 s p95. As failures built up, payments-api's provider circuit breaker (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on) opened at about 18:54:20Z. Since then nearly every POST /payments returns an immediate 503 ('/v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open') and leaves the payment pending. That is the 97% 5xx rate. The breaker is doing its job. Nothing shows a change of ours as the trigger: the whole stack was created together at 18:52:28-29Z, about 2.5 minutes before the alert, which looks like a fresh test run, perhaps with a fault injected at the provider. Why the provider fails is not visible, since it sends us no logs.

evidence.shows: POST /payments: 201s fall from 3.38/s (18:53:51) to 0 (18:54:51), and 503s rise from about 0.1/s to 5.89/s (18:54:21), then 12.71/s (18:54:51). 409s rise slightly, to 0.1/s.

Every recent payments-api ERROR line is 'provider unavailable; payment left pending' with '/v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open'. The breaker is open, and payments such as pmt_000423-437 stay pending.

Provider calls that got an HTTP answer include 500s at 0.27-0.40/s from 18:52:57Z, alongside 200s. All client calls fall to 0 by 18:54:57. No ReadTimeout series appears, so this metric does not count timeouts.

Trace for pmt_000252 (9.64 s, 503): Redis and Postgres spans take under 2 ms each. Three POSTs to http://fake-provider:8000/v1/payments each end in httpx ReadTimeout after about 3.0 s. The time is spent at the provider.
Slow POST /payments traces at 18:53:58-18:54:04Z last about 3.0, 6.2 and 9.6 s, matching 1-3 timed-out attempts of about 3 s each.
Provider calls that did return were fast, with a p95 of about 5-8 ms for both 200 and 500. The provider either answered at once or hung until our timeout.
Provider attempts rise to about 3.9/s at 18:53:52-18:54:07, then fall to about 0.08/s by 18:55:07. Only the breaker's trial calls are left.

All containers, fake-provider included, were created at 18:52:28-29Z from the same image. payments-api settings are PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=returned. There is no later deploy of ours to undo.

proposed_fix.summary: Do not roll back or restart our services: nothing of ours changed, and the breaker is protecting us. Keep the breaker on, and watch whether its trial calls start succeeding, through payments-api provider client metrics and the 201 rate. Escalate to, or check, the provider side (fault injection, if this is a test run). After the provider recovers, run the money check: reconcile the payments left pending, and above all those whose calls timed out, because the provider may have charged them even though we never saw an answer, and the retries could have created duplicate charges. Confirm whether payments-api sends an idempotency key to the provider. Also confirm that timeouts get recorded in the http_client metrics.

diagnosis.blast_radius: This fix changes nothing in the system, so it carries no direct risk. Until the provider recovers, POST /payments keeps failing fast with 503, and payments pile up as pending. If timed-out calls were charged at the provider, our books and theirs differ until they are reconciled. With synthetic data, no real customer or money is affected.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Nothing is changed, so there is nothing to undo. If the breaker's behaviour itself turns out to be wrong, for example if it fails to close after the provider recovers, it can be revisited then through a human-approved config change or restart.
